# (7) Loop Vectorization

## Dependence-based legality analysis

Loop vectorization transforms a scalar loop body executing one iteration at a time into a loop body that processes VF (vectorization factor) iterations simultaneously using SIMD instructions. Legality rests on data dependence analysis, classically formalized in the polyhedral/dependence-vector framework (Allen & Kennedy, Wolfe). For a pair of array references in a loop nest, the compiler computes a **distance vector** (the difference in loop iteration counts between a dependent write and the subsequent read/write) or, when distances aren't compile-time constant, a **direction vector** (each component taking values `<`, `=`, `>`, or `*` indicating whether the dependent iteration occurs before, same as, or after in that loop dimension). Classic tests used to derive these include the **GCD test** (checks divisibility conditions on subscript coefficients to rule out integer solutions), the **Banerjee test** (bounds-based inequality test using the extreme values subscripts can take), and for loops with affine subscripts, exact integer programming or the **Omega test**.

For a single loop to be vectorizable along its own dimension, the key legality condition is the absence of a **loop-carried dependence with a direction that is backward and a distance smaller than VF** in a way that crosses the simultaneously-executed iteration group. Concretely: a dependence with distance ≥ VF (or direction `<` meaning it only flows forward across later iterations beyond the vectorized group) is safe; a true (flow) dependence with a small positive distance (e.g. distance 1, as in `a[i] = a[i-1] + x[i]`) is **loop-carried and distance-bound**, forcing either serialization, a smaller VF, or a different transformation. Anti-dependences and output dependences (WAR, WAW) are generally benign for vectorization because SIMD lanes execute "logically in parallel" with all loads for an iteration group semantically preceding all stores; only true RAW dependences with short carried distance, or any dependence whose direction indicates one lane must observe a value written by a "later" lane, block straightforward SIMDization. When dependence distance cannot be proven safely, compilers emit a **runtime memory dependence check** (array bounds/overlap check between pointers, i.e., a runtime alias test) and generate two versions: a vectorized loop guarded by the check and a scalar fallback — this is the dependence analysis combined with multi-versioning.

## SLP vs. loop vectorization

**Loop vectorization** (traditional, Allen-Kennedy-style) packs the *same scalar operation* across *successive iterations* of a loop into one vector instruction — the vector lanes correspond to iteration index `i, i+1, …, i+VF-1`.

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization**, introduced by Larsen & Amarasinghe, instead finds *isomorphic independent scalar instructions within a single basic block* (often within one loop iteration, or in straight-line code with no loop at all) and packs them into vector instructions. SLP builds candidate "packs" starting from adjacent memory accesses (seed pairs, e.g. `a[i]` and `a[i+1]` loaded in the same iteration for a 4-wide unrolled body) and grows them by following the def-use chains of isomorphic operations, checking that operands can be packed consistently, inserting shuffles/permutes where lanes don't naturally align. SLP is complementary to loop vectorization: many compilers (LLVM's SLPVectorizer, GCC's tree-ssa SLP) first apply loop unrolling to expose multiple iterations as straight-line isomorphic statements, then run SLP across that enlarged body, which can vectorize patterns loop-vectorization alone would miss (e.g., struct-of-arrays versus array-of-structs mixed shuffles, or vectorizing a loop with VF less than the hardware width by combining it with same-block isomorphic work).

## Peeling, masking/predication, alignment

Loop trip counts are rarely exact multiples of VF, requiring handling of the **remainder loop**. **Loop peeling** strips off a prologue or epilogue of scalar iterations: a prologue peel can also be used for **alignment handling** — peeling off iterations before the loop body until the vectorized memory accesses reach a hardware-preferred alignment boundary (e.g., 16/32/64-byte aligned loads/stores), avoiding slower unaligned vector load/store instructions or satisfying ISA requirements for aligned-only instructions. A separate, epilogue peel (or a scalar remainder loop) handles the tail iterations that don't fill a full vector.

**Masking/predication** is the alternative to peeling for the remainder (and increasingly the primary mechanism on ISAs with predicated execution, e.g. AVX-512 mask registers, ARM SVE predicates): the compiler generates a single vectorized loop body executed with a **lane mask** that disables (predicates off) lanes corresponding to out-of-range iterations on the final iteration, eliminating the separate scalar remainder loop entirely. Predication also handles **control flow inside the loop body** — if-conversion transforms conditional scalar statements into predicated vector operations (e.g., `vpblendvb`/select instructions, or masked loads/stores) so that divergent branches within the vectorized region become straight-line code with per-lane masks, which is necessary because SIMD lanes cannot independently branch.

## Reduction vectorization and idiom recognition

A **reduction** combines loop iteration values into a scalar accumulator via an associative (and often commutative) operator — sum, product, min, max, bitwise AND/OR/XOR. Naively this is a loop-carried dependence (the accumulator read-modify-write chain) that appears to block vectorization. The compiler recognizes the **reduction idiom** structurally (a single commutative/associative operator combining the loop-carried PHI node with a loop-invariant-free operand) and vectorizes by maintaining VF **partial accumulators in a vector register**, combining per-iteration-group values into the vector accumulator, and performing a final **horizontal reduction** (a cross-lane reduce, e.g. a sequence of shuffle+add instructions, or a dedicated horizontal-add instruction) after the loop to collapse the vector accumulator to the scalar result. This relies on treating floating-point addition as associative for vectorization purposes, which technically changes rounding behavior — hence compilers only do it under relaxed floating-point semantics (`-ffast-math`, or explicit reduction pragmas like OpenMP's `reduction` clause or `#pragma omp simd reduction`) unless the target type is integer. Related idiom recognition includes detecting **min/max idioms** (compare-and-select patterns), **dot-product idioms**, and **population count / find-first-set idioms**, which some vectorizers map directly to dedicated vector instructions.

## Cost modeling and VF/interleaving selection

Vectorization is profitable only when estimated vector cost beats estimated scalar cost, since vectorization incurs overhead: shuffles/permutes for non-contiguous or misaligned access, mask generation, horizontal reductions, and potential underutilization. Compilers build a **cost model** that sums per-instruction costs (load/store, arithmetic, shuffle, mask-blend) for the scalar loop body versus each candidate vectorized version, weighted by estimated trip count, and picks the configuration with lowest cost per scalar iteration. This governs both **VF selection** — iterating over legal vectorization factors (bounded by target vector register width divided by element size, e.g. 4 for `float` with 128-bit SSE, 8 with 256-bit AVX2) and selecting the one with best cost — and the **interleaving factor** (also called unroll factor within the vectorizer), which replicates the vectorized body multiple times to increase instruction-level parallelism and hide vector instruction latency, hiding load-use latency and improving scheduling at the cost of larger code size and register pressure.

## Gather/scatter and strided access

When memory accesses inside the loop are not unit-stride contiguous — e.g., `a[idx[i]]` (indirect/indexed access) or `a[i*stride]` with stride > 1 — the compiler cannot use a simple contiguous vector load/store. **Gather** instructions (e.g., `vpgatherdd`) load VF elements from VF independently computed addresses into one vector register in a single instruction; **scatter** instructions do the inverse for stores. These are supported natively on AVX2 (gather only), AVX-512, and SVE (both gather and scatter), but carry higher latency and lower throughput than contiguous accesses, which the cost model must account for. For known constant **strided access**, an alternative to gather/scatter is **strided load/store lowering via shuffle**: load several contiguous cache lines and use shuffle/permute instructions to deinterleave the strided elements into separate vectors (common for structure-of-arrays access with small fixed stride, e.g. de-interleaving RGB or complex-number interleaved data), which can outperform gather/scatter when the stride is small and compile-time known.

---

# (8) General Loop Optimizations

## Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)

LICM identifies computations inside a loop body whose operands are all **loop-invariant** — defined outside the loop, or themselves invariant computations — and hoists them to the loop preheader (a single-entry block executed exactly once before the loop), so they execute once instead of once per iteration. Legality requires that the hoisted instruction has no side effects dependent on loop-varying state, and for hoisting loads, that the memory location is not modified anywhere in the loop (checked via alias analysis) and that the load is safe to speculatively execute on every path (or guarded by analysis showing the loop executes at least once, or sunk back on a path where execution would not have reached it, to avoid introducing a fault that wasn't present in the original program — notably for loads that may trap or divide instructions that may divide-by-zero). LICM is typically implemented on SSA form by walking the loop in dominance order and moving candidate instructions whose operands dominate the loop header to the preheader; sinking (the dual operation, moving invariant stores/final values to the loop exit) is handled by related passes.

## Loop unrolling and unroll-and-jam

**Full unrolling** replicates the entire loop body for every iteration of a loop with a known, small, compile-time-constant trip count, eliminating the loop control overhead (branch, induction variable increment, trip count comparison) entirely and exposing more instructions for scheduling and other optimizations.

**Partial unrolling** replicates the body a fixed **unroll factor** (U) times inside the loop, decrementing the trip count by U per iteration and adding a remainder loop (or further peeling) for leftover iterations when the trip count isn't a multiple of U. The unroll factor is selected by a cost model balancing reduced loop overhead and increased instruction-level parallelism/scheduling freedom against code size growth (instruction cache pressure) and increased register pressure (more live ranges from the replicated body competing for a fixed register file).

**Unroll-and-jam** (also called "register tiling") applies to a loop *nest*: it unrolls an outer loop by factor U and then **fuses (jams)** the U replicated copies of the inner loop body back into a single inner loop, producing an inner loop body that computes U outer-iterations' worth of work per inner iteration. This increases reuse of values loaded in the inner loop across the U unrolled outer iterations (improving register-level data reuse and enabling SIMD/ILP), and is legal only when the fusion of the U inner loop copies doesn't violate dependences between them (dependence distance in the outer loop dimension must not create a forward reference the fused order violates).

## Loop fusion and loop fission/distribution

**Loop fusion** (loop jamming) merges two adjacent loops with conforming iteration spaces into a single loop, executing both bodies per iteration. Benefits: reduced loop overhead, and critically, increased **temporal locality and reuse** when both loops touch the same data (fusing eliminates a second pass over an array, keeping it in cache rather than reloading from memory). Legality requires that fusing doesn't invert dependences — specifically no dependence should exist from a statement in the second loop's iteration `i` to a statement in the first loop's iteration `j > i`, which the compiler checks via dependence testing across the two loops' iteration spaces.

**Loop fission** (loop distribution) is the dual: splitting one loop into multiple loops, each handling a subset of the original body's statements, executed over the same iteration range. This is used when the combined loop can't be vectorized or has conflicting resource/dependence requirements as a whole, but one of the split-out sub-loops can be vectorized or optimized independently (e.g., splitting out a reduction into its own loop, or isolating a statement with a problematic dependence so the remaining loop is dependence-free). Legality again requires preserving all cross-statement dependences, typically satisfied by assigning statements to fission groups respecting a topological order of the dependence graph.

## Loop interchange

**Loop interchange** swaps the nesting order of two loops in a perfectly (or nearly perfectly) nested loop, most commonly to improve **spatial locality** by making the innermost loop stride through memory contiguously (e.g., converting a column-major-stride inner loop in a row-major array into a unit-stride inner loop) and thereby reducing cache misses and improving prefetcher effectiveness, and/or to expose the loop with the richest parallelism/vectorization opportunity as the innermost loop.

Legality is determined by the **dependence direction vector matrix** for the nest: interchange is legal if, after permuting the corresponding entries of every dependence direction vector to the new nesting order, no direction vector becomes "illegal" — specifically, a direction vector must not have its leading nonzero `>` ("backward") component moved to a position before a `<` would be required, i.e. the classic rule is that interchange is illegal if some dependence has direction vector with a `<` in the position of the loop being moved innermost while a `>` precedes it improperly; more operationally, Wolfe/Banerjee's interchange legality test checks each dependence's direction vector doesn't contain the forbidden pattern `(..., '>', ..., '<', ...)` relative to the new order that would make the transformed program execute a dependent write after its dependent read.

## Loop tiling / blocking

**Tiling** (blocking) partitions the iteration space of a loop nest into smaller rectangular (or more generally, hyperrectangular) blocks ("tiles"), restructuring the nest so an outer pair of loops strides over tiles and an inner pair iterates within a tile. The tile size is chosen so that the working set touched within one tile (across all arrays referenced) fits in a target cache level (L1 or L2), maximizing reuse of data while it's resident in cache before moving to the next tile — this directly targets **capacity misses** in loops that otherwise reuse data across a working set larger than cache capacity (classic example: matrix multiplication, where naive triple-nested loops thrash cache on large matrices, but tiling restores near-peak reuse). Tiling is legal for any affine loop nest and doesn't itself change dependences as long as the tile traversal order is still a valid topological order of the original iteration space's dependences (a rectangular tiling of a nest with only "forward" dependences within tiles, or careful skewing for nests with cross-tile dependences, preserves correctness).

## Loop strength reduction

**Strength reduction** replaces expensive operations inside a loop with cheaper equivalent ones, exploiting the structure of **induction variables** (variables that vary by a fixed amount each iteration). The canonical case: an array-indexing expression like `a[i * k]` inside a loop recomputes a multiplication every iteration; strength reduction introduces a new induction variable `j` initialized to 0 before the loop and incremented by `k` each iteration (`j += k`), replacing the multiplication with an addition, since `j` tracks `i*k` exactly. More generally this applies to any linear function of the basic induction variable (`c1*i + c2`), turning repeated multiplication into repeated addition, and is especially impactful for address computations in pointer-chasing-free array loops, converting `base + i*stride` address arithmetic into incrementally updated pointers.

## Induction variable analysis and canonicalization

**Induction variable (IV) analysis** identifies all variables in a loop that evolve as an affine (or more general chain-of-recurrence) function of the loop trip count — classified as **basic induction variables** (incremented by a loop-invariant amount each iteration, e.g. the raw loop counter) and **derived induction variables** (expressible as an affine function of a basic IV, e.g. `j = a*i + b`). Canonicalization introduces (or recognizes and normalizes to) a single **canonical induction variable**: one that starts at 0 and increments by 1 each iteration, giving every other IV a simple affine representation relative to it. This canonical form is what SSA-based compilers typically materialize as a loop's `%indvar` with an associated `%indvar.next = add %indvar, 1`, simplifying downstream analyses (trip count computation, dependence testing, strength reduction, and vectorization's VF-based indexing) because all derived accesses reduce to affine expressions of one normalized variable, and it enables **linear function test replacement**, where loop exit conditions originally tested on a derived IV are rewritten to test the canonical IV directly, allowing the derived IV's computation to be eliminated entirely if otherwise unused (induction variable elimination / dead IV removal).

## Loop unswitching

**Loop unswitching** hoists a loop-invariant conditional branch (a branch whose condition doesn't depend on any loop-varying value) out of the loop body, duplicating the loop into two versions — one for each branch outcome — wrapped by the hoisted `if`. Concretely, `for (i...) { if (invariant_cond) A(i); else B(i); }` becomes `if (invariant_cond) { for (i...) A(i); } else { for (i...) B(i); }`. This eliminates the per-iteration branch (and its associated misprediction risk and control-flow overhead) and, critically, produces two simplified loop bodies each free of the conditional, which independently become more amenable to further optimization — particularly vectorization, since the removed branch may have been blocking SIMDization via control-flow divergence. The cost is code duplication (loop body appears twice), so compilers apply it selectively based on estimated code-size growth versus the benefit of removing invariant branching from the hot path.
